title: Message Documentation and Routing Clinical Concerns

sections.learningObjectives:
- Document phone messages accurately, capturing who, what, when, and callback details in the caller's own words.
- Route clinical concerns and medication or results questions to licensed staff while staying within the assistant's scope of practice.
- Apply read-back of names, numbers, and medication names to verify accuracy before ending a call.
- Produce complete, objective, legible, and time-stamped message entries that support timely follow-up.
- Recognize urgent and emergent concerns and escalate them promptly through the office chain of command or emergency protocol.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A complete message is like a full address on an envelope: it needs the who, what, when, and how-to-reach-you or the letter may never get where it needs to go.

### Question 2

Writing the date and time is like putting a timestamp on a homework assignment: it shows when the work arrived so everyone knows what happened when.

### Question 3

Reading a number back is like repeating an address to a delivery driver before they leave, so you both know it is right.

### Question 4

Names are like fingerprints: two people can sound alike but be spelled completely differently, so you ask to be sure.

### Question 5

You write down what the caller actually said, like taking notes on what a friend tells you, instead of guessing what they meant.

### Question 6

Ink is like writing a test answer you cannot erase, so everyone can read exactly what was written.

### Question 7

You write down the facts of what happened, not your guess about what is wrong, just like a referee records the play, not their opinion.

### Question 8

Signing your work is like putting your name on a group project so the teacher knows who did that part.

### Question 9

Using name and birth date is like matching a locker number and name before opening it, so you grab the right one.

### Question 10

You send the question to the person trained to answer it, like asking the math teacher a math question instead of the gym teacher.

### Question 11

You pass the question to the doctor or nurse, like handing a tricky question to the teacher instead of guessing the answer.

### Question 12

Some messages are like a fire alarm: when they go off, you act right away instead of finishing your snack.

### Question 13

Read-back is like repeating an order at a restaurant so the cook makes exactly what you asked for.

### Question 14

When you are not sure, you ask the grown-up in charge instead of making up an answer.

### Question 15

Write down what happened, not what you think about it, like a camera recording a scene without adding commentary.

### Question 16

Writing the time is like checking the clock when an emergency starts so you know how fast help arrived.

### Question 17

Talking about a patient's private business where others can hear is like reading someone's diary out loud in a classroom.

### Question 18

A form is like a checklist for packing: it makes sure you do not forget anything important.

### Question 19

Writing and repeating a phone number is like carefully copying a code and checking each character.

### Question 20

Medicine questions go to the medicine experts, like asking the librarian for a book instead of the bus driver.

### Question 21

Writing down both people is like noting who dropped off a note and who it is about.

### Question 22

Writing down who you gave the note to is like a delivery receipt showing the package reached the right person.

### Question 23

You would not promise to deliver a message at an exact minute if you could not be sure; you just say you will pass it along.

### Question 24

Your job is to be a careful messenger who takes a clear note and hands it to the doctor or nurse.

### Question 25

No matter how busy it gets, the assistant passes the question to the trained expert, like a relay runner handing off the baton.

### Question 26

Answering 'What time do you close?' yourself is fine, but a question about symptoms goes to the nurse, like sorting easy and hard questions.

### Question 27

Private information is only shared with people the patient has said it is okay to share with, like a secret you keep for a friend.

### Question 28

A refill is like a permission slip that only the teacher (the clinician) can sign; you deliver the request.

### Question 29

Test results are like a sealed report card that the teacher, not the student helper, reads and explains.

### Question 30

Medicine names can sound alike, so you ask the caller to spell it, like double-checking a tricky word in a spelling bee.

### Question 31

You ask the follow-up questions a detective would ask: where and when, to give the doctor a fuller picture.

### Question 32

Objective means writing down just the facts, like a referee reporting what happened without taking sides.

### Question 33

Fix a mistake with one clean line, like crossing out a wrong answer and writing the right one next to it, so everyone sees what changed.

### Question 34

Even if a detail is missing, you keep the note and flag what is missing, like keeping a homework page with one blank answer.

### Question 35

Messy handwriting is like a blurry photo of an address: you might deliver to the wrong house.

### Question 36

You write down what the person needs help with, even if they are upset, like helping someone who is crying tell you what happened.

### Question 37

On voicemail, say just enough to ask for a call back, like leaving a note that says 'call me' instead of the whole story.

### Question 38

A call like this is a true emergency; you get help right away, like calling a lifeguard when someone is in trouble in the water.

### Question 39

Writing down what happened next is like finishing a story so everyone knows how it ended.

### Question 40

Emergent is like a fire right now; urgent is like a leak that needs fixing soon.

### Question 41

Checking the birth date is like checking both the name and the locker number so you open the right one.

### Question 42

You quote what the person said, like repeating a friend's exact words instead of a made-up summary.

### Question 43

A side effect is reported to the doctor, like telling the coach about a pain instead of deciding to sit out on your own.

### Question 44

Both names are like listing who sent and who received a package so you can track it if it is lost.

### Question 45

You sort messages like a nurse sorting patients: the most serious need goes first.

### Question 46

The correct notes are facts; the wrong note is an opinion, like writing 'he is being dramatic' instead of 'he said his knee hurts.'

### Question 47

These are emergency signs, like a smoke alarm, and you get help right away.

### Question 48

Fill in the blank spaces while the person is still on the line, like asking for the missing address before the mail carrier leaves.

### Question 49

Write it down right away, like jotting a note the moment you remember it so you do not forget.

### Question 50

The doctor needs to know exactly how the person is doing now, like describing how a plant is wilting so the gardener knows what to fix.

### Question 51

You say the number back and the caller says 'yes, that's right,' like checking a code before you lock it in.

### Question 52

Write what you can see or hear them say, not what you guess they feel, like reporting a player's score, not your mood about it.

### Question 53

Pass along exactly what the doctor said, like delivering a note without rewriting it.

### Question 54

If you cannot hear clearly, you ask the person to say it again, like asking a friend to repeat a muffled message.

### Question 55

Use words everyone knows, like using full street names on a sign so no one gets lost.

### Question 56

The best note has all the pieces, like a complete recipe with every ingredient listed.

### Question 57

The assistant is like a receptionist who takes the question to the doctor rather than reading the X-ray themselves.

### Question 58

Closed-loop is like saying 'got it' and repeating the plan so both people are sure they agree.

### Question 59

Give the message to the person with the right training, like handing homework to the correct teacher.

### Question 60

Copy the exact words like a direct quote, so nothing important gets changed by accident.

### Question 61

You still pass along the important message, but you honestly note that the person did not give a name.

### Question 62

Knowing how fast something is changing tells the doctor how worried to be, like knowing how fast a leak is growing.

### Question 63

Keep private notes in a locked drawer, not out on a table where everyone can see.

### Question 64

If you do not know a word, you ask what it means instead of pretending you understood.

### Question 65

Put a bright 'URGENT' sticker and the time on it, like marking a package 'fragile' and noting when it was sent.

### Question 66

You deliver the message word-for-word, like reading a note the doctor wrote, without adding your own ideas.

### Question 67

Leave out your personal thoughts and keep only the useful facts, like a news reporter sticking to the story.

### Question 68

Check both the name and the birth date, like matching a key to the right lock before opening.

### Question 69

A sick, sleepy child with a high fever needs the doctor's attention quickly, so you pass the message right away.

### Question 70

Facts like 'she said the pain is 7 out of 10' are objective; guesses about severity are not.

### Question 71

Writing only 'there is a problem' is like calling for help without saying where or what the emergency is.

### Question 72

If the first person is unavailable, you go to the next person in charge, like telling another teacher when yours is out.

### Question 73

You take the question to the doctor or nurse, like asking the coach whether a player needs to see the trainer.

### Question 74

The note is missing the address parts, like an envelope with a message but no name or address.

### Question 75

Repeat the main points back, like saying 'so you mean...' to check you got the story right.

### Question 76

Sudden loss of sight is like a flashing emergency light; you act immediately.

### Question 77

Handle the part you are trained for and pass the rest to the expert, like answering the easy questions and forwarding the hard ones.

### Question 78

Throat tightness is a true emergency, like a smoke alarm that means act now.

### Question 79

Confirm who you are talking to before sharing private details, like checking a name badge before opening the door.

### Question 80

Two swapped digits send the call to the wrong person, like mailing a letter to the wrong house number.

### Question 81

This is the most urgent kind of call, like shouting for help when someone has fallen and will not wake.

### Question 82

Check off every needed detail before saying goodbye, like making sure you packed everything before leaving.

### Question 83

The doctor needs a working phone number and a note saying how urgent it is, like a return address and a 'priority' stamp.

### Question 84

Breathing trouble that is getting worse fast needs help right now, like a balloon losing air quickly.

### Question 85

Checking your work with the caller, like double-checking a spelling before writing it down, prevents mistakes.
